summary: Defines the scenarios in which IPv6 transition mechanisms are meant to be used in unmanaged networks, typically home or small office networks. Scenarios are specific to one subnet and described by the IP connectivity offered by the gateway and the ISP. The aim is to help evaluate which transition mechanisms suit them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3750 sets out the situations an IPv6 transition mechanism has to work in when the network is a home or small office network that nobody administers. It describes the four kinds of application that run in such a network, what each of them needs from IPv6, and how the answers change as the gateway and the internet provider gain IPv6 support one stage at a time.

questions: what is an unmanaged network in ipv6 terms
why does ipv6 transition need tunnels in home networks
subtitle: What IPv6 transition has to cope with in a home or small office network

tldr.problem: Transition mechanisms from IPv4 to IPv6 are usually judged against the needs of large networks, but the first adopters of IPv6 are home and small office networks whose gateway nobody administers.
tldr.mechanism: The document fixes the setting as a single-subnet network with one ISP link and a gateway that may translate addresses, then works out what local, client, peer-to-peer and server applications need from IPv6, and maps those needs onto four deployment cases depending on what the gateway and the ISP support.
tldr.outcome: It is a scenarios paper. It recommends that unmanaged networks not run protocol translation for them, and that the tunnel mechanisms that carry IPv6 over IPv4 be designed for safe use.

facts.value: 27, from the provider, the gateway and the hosts each being IPv4-only, dual-stack or IPv6-only

facts.value: Unmanaged networks should allow hosts that choose to use them

today: RFC 3750 is an Informational memo published in April 2004, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a scenarios document: it compares transition mechanisms against the four cases in a companion evaluation draft rather than defining a mechanism itself.

sections.title: What the Document Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
To evaluate the suitability of transition mechanisms from IPv4 to IPv6, the environment in which those mechanisms have to be used has to be defined. One specific scope is the unmanaged network, which typically corresponds to a home network or a small office network.

The document studies the requirements posed by various transition scenarios and is organised into four main parts. It defines the topology under consideration, presents the four classes of applications considered for unmanaged networks, studies the requirements of those classes, and analyses how the requirements translate into four configurations expected during IPv6 deployment: gateways that do not provide IPv6, dual-stack gateways connected to dual-stack providers, dual-stack gateways connected to IPv4-only providers, and IPv6-capable gateways connected to IPv6-only providers. The four configurations are not an exhaustive list of possibilities, but the authors believe they represent the common cases for unmanaged networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Before asking whether a transition technique works, the document fixes the scene: a small network with no administrator. Everything that follows is about that scene.

sections.title: The Typical Unmanaged Network
sections.content:
The typical unmanaged network is composed of a single subnet connected to the Internet through a single internet service provider connection, with several hosts attached to the subnet. Between the subnet and the access link is a gateway, which may or may not perform NAT and firewall functions. When the gateway performs NAT it generally allocates private IPv4 addresses to the local hosts.

A key point of this configuration is that the gateway is typically not managed. In most cases it is a simple appliance that incorporates some static policies, and there are many cases in which the gateway is procured and configured by the provider. The document notes cases of two gateways back to back, one managed by the provider and the other added by the owner of the network, and does not cover them because most require some management, or the user's gateway can act as a layer 2 switch. The access link might be a static permanent connection or a dynamic one such as a dial-up or ISDN line, and in a degenerate case an unmanaged network consists of a single host connected directly to a provider.

Some cases replace the gateway with a layer 2 bridge, so that the hosts have direct access to the provider service; the document treats these as if the gateway were not present. The definition of unmanaged networks explicitly excludes networks composed of multiple subnets. Some home and small business networks do have multiple subnets, but in the current state of the technology those are not unmanaged, because some competent administrator has to configure the routers, so the document concentrates on single-subnet networks where no such operator is expected.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture is a single home subnet behind one box that the internet provider usually supplied and nobody configures. If the box is missing, the computers are treated as if they were plugged into the provider directly.

sections.title: Four Classes of Application
sections.content:
Four types of application are considered.

Local applications involve only the hosts that are part of the unmanaged network, with file sharing or printer sharing as typical examples. They work effectively in IPv4 unmanaged networks even when the gateway performs NAT or firewall functions, and the firewall services at the gateway are often deemed desirable because they isolate the local applications from interference by Internet users.

Client applications involve a client on the unmanaged network and a server at a remote location, such as accessing a web server from inside the network or reading and sending e-mail with the help of a server outside it. They tend to work correctly in IPv4 unmanaged networks even when the gateway performs NAT or firewall functions, because those translation and firewall functions are designed precisely to enable client applications.

Peer-to-peer applications, in the sense the document uses the term, involve hosts on the unmanaged network and hosts outside it. They often do not work well in unmanaged IPv4 networks, and application developers often have to enlist the help of a relay server, in effect restructuring the peer-to-peer connection into a pair of back-to-back client/server connections.

Server applications involve running a server in the unmanaged network for use by other parties outside the network, such as a web server or an e-mail server. Deploying these servers in most unmanaged IPv4 networks requires special programming of the NAT or firewall, and is more complex when the NAT publishes only a small number of global addresses and relies on port translation, because in the common case of a single global address a given external port can only be used by one internal server. Deploying servers also usually requires giving each server a stable DNS name and associating a global IPv4 address with it, whether that address belongs to the server itself or to the router acting as a firewall or NAT. Since updating DNS is a management task, it falls somewhat outside the scope of an unmanaged network, although out-of-band techniques such as passing the address around in an instant message are possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sorts the programs people run into four kinds: those that stay inside the house, those that talk to a server elsewhere, those that talk directly to another person, and those that serve other people from inside the house. Each kind survives the current arrangement of the home gateway in a different way.

sections.title: What the Applications Need
sections.content:
As the transition to IPv6 happens, the requirements of the various applications have to be met. Applications that worked well with IPv4 should continue to work well during the transition, it should be possible to use IPv6 to deploy new applications that are currently hard to deploy in IPv4 networks, and the deployment of these applications should be simple and easy to manage while also being robust and secure. The requirements fall into three categories: connectivity, naming and security.

Connectivity issues include the provision of IPv6 addresses and their quality: do hosts need global addresses, should those addresses be stable, and what should the expected lifetimes be? Naming issues cover the management of names for the hosts: do hosts need DNS names, and is inverse name resolution a requirement? Security issues include possible restriction of connectivity, privacy concerns, and the security of the applications themselves.

Local applications require local connectivity and must keep working even if the unmanaged network is isolated from the Internet, and they typically use ad hoc naming systems, many of them proprietary, with the service location protocol given as an example of a standard one. Their security is usually improved if they can be isolated from the global Internet.

Client applications require global connectivity, and in an IPv6 network the client would be expected to use a global IPv6 address that stays stable for the duration of the session. They typically use DNS to locate servers, and in an IPv6 network the client must be able to locate a DNS resolver. Many servers look up a DNS name associated with the client's IP address, and in IPv4 that address is often allocated by the provider to the gateway, with a perfunctory PTR record maintained by the provider; whether an equivalent function should be provided in IPv6 is unclear.

Peer-to-peer applications also require global connectivity with a stable global address for the duration of the session. Assuming the peers have safely exchanged their IPv6 addresses, the main security requirement is the ability to exchange data between them without interference by third parties. The document reports that many individuals would be willing to consider an IPv6-only model if they could get two guarantees: no regression from IPv4, so that every customer who could take part using IPv4 can also be reached by IPv6, and that IPv6 solves at least some of their hard problems, such as letting peers behind an IPv4 NAT take part.

Server applications require global connectivity, which in IPv6 implies global addresses. In an IPv4 network using NAT, each service has to be configured on the NAT to forward packets to the server offering it. Server applications normally rely on publishing the server's address in DNS, which requires the server to be provisioned with a global DNS name, and the DNS entries have to be updated, preferably in real time, if the address changes. In practice updating DNS can be slow, so server applications have a better chance of being deployed if the IPv6 addresses remain stable.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of application needs something slightly different: a way to reach the outside, a way to be found, and protection. Servers that publish their address need that address to stay the same, because changing a name in DNS is a job nobody does at home.

sections.title: Four Cases of IPv6 Deployment
sections.content:
Deployment is expected to proceed from an initial state with little or no IPv6 to a final stage in which the IPv4 infrastructure might be retired, stretching over many years and not synchronised, as different parties deploy at different paces. Three entities are distinguished: the provider, possibly including the consumer premises equipment, the home gateway, and the hosts. Each can be IPv4-only, dual-stack or IPv6-only, which gives 27 possibilities, of which four are described: a gateway that does not provide IPv6 at all; a dual-stack gateway connected to a dual-stack provider; a dual-stack gateway connected to an IPv4-only provider; and a gateway connected to an IPv6-only provider.

In case A the gateway does not provide IPv6, so the hosts have to handle the transition mechanisms themselves. The focus is on reaching IPv6-only hosts outside the network, and the document expects peer-to-peer applications to be the primary early motivation, because they are deployed in a coordinated fashion, so that hosts can all receive some form of IPv6 upgrade, and they often provide their own naming infrastructure and so do not depend on DNS services. If the local gateway gives out global IPv4 addresses, the hosts can exercise the mechanisms of case C individually; if it performs NAT, a mechanism is needed that tunnels over a protocol that can easily traverse NAT, either TCP or preferably UDP, since tunnelling over TCP can perform poorly when time-outs and retransmissions occur.

In case B the provider and the gateway are both dual stack, and the gateway can use native IPv6 connectivity and an IPv6 prefix allocated by the provider. Client, peer-to-peer and server applications can all be enabled easily. The document's conclusion is that unmanaged networks should not have to provide translation services, and it gives the arguments: against translation, it is hard to provide such services for all applications compared with the relative ease of installing dual-stack solutions, whether by application relays or by network level services, since network level translation must be complemented by application layer gateways that rewrite references to IP addresses, and deciding when to translate DNS requests has proven very difficult. For translation, its availability would accelerate the deployment of IPv6-only devices, but it would also reduce the pressure to provide IPv6 at all.

In case C the gateway is dual stack but the provider is not, so the gateway cannot rely on the provider for IPv6 connectivity. The application support is identical to case B. The gateway behaves as an IPv6 router and the nodes obtain IPv4 addresses, IPv6 link local addresses and IPv6 global addresses. Two ways bring immediate IPv6 connectivity on top of an IPv4-only infrastructure: automatic tunnels, such as those provided by 6to4, or configured tunnels.

In case D the provider is IPv6-only, so the gateway loses IPv4 connectivity and the network includes IPv4-only, IPv6-only and dual-stack hosts. Any interaction between hosts in the unmanaged network and IPv4 hosts on the Internet requires inter-protocol services from the provider. There are three ways the provider could give the network access to IPv4 applications: a set of application relays, an address translation service, or IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnels. The analysis concludes that a tunnel service is vastly preferable, because relays would have to exist for every application and would only be reachable over IPv6, so the legacy IPv4-only hosts could not use them, and translation carries the same problems as in case B.
sections.plainLanguage: The document walks through four stages: a gateway that knows nothing about IPv6, a gateway and a provider that both speak it, a gateway that speaks it while the provider does not, and finally a provider that has switched over. In each case it asks what the home user can actually run, and it settles on tunnels rather than translation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations are discussed as part of the applications' requirements, and the document lists them. There is the guarantee that local applications are only used locally, the protection of the privacy of clients, the requirement that peer-to-peer connections are only used by authorised peers, the requirement that tunnelling protocols used for IPv6 access over IPv4 be designed for secure use, and the related requirement that servers in the infrastructure supporting transition scenarios be designed so as not to be vulnerable to abuse.

The privacy requirement of client applications receives more detail in section 4.2.1. Whether the IPv6 service should be engineered to enhance client privacy, and whether support for RFC 3041 should be required, is debatable. RFC 3041 lets hosts pick IPv6 addresses in which the host identifier is randomised, which was designed to make sure that addresses and host identifiers cannot be used to track the connections of a device's owner. Many observe that randomising the host identifier is only a half measure: if the unmanaged network's address prefix remains constant, the randomisation only hides which host in the network originated a given connection, which places the privacy rating of such connections on a par with IPv4 connections from a network where a NAT manages a static address, because in both cases the address or prefix identifies the network itself.

The randomisation does provide benefits. It destroys any correlation between the addresses used at various locations for mobile hosts, and it removes information that could be extracted from a hardwired host identifier, such as a serial number that could be tied to a brand of equipment. Randomisation of addresses is not sufficient to guarantee privacy, since usage can be tracked in many other ways, from application level cookies to traffic analysis, but the document argues that this is no reason to enable additional tracking through IPv6 addresses. It has costs: address management in hosts is more complex, reverse DNS services are harder to provide, and the gateway may have to keep a larger cache of neighbour addresses. Given the limited benefits it would be unreasonable to require that all hosts use privacy addresses, and given the limited costs it is reasonable to require that all unmanaged networks allow the use of privacy addresses by those hosts that choose to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks that the network be able to hide which computer inside the house a connection came from, and it settles on allowing hosts that want it to use randomised addresses, without making everyone do so.

items.title: Local applications
items.text: File or printer sharing between hosts inside the network. They work today because the firewall in the gateway isolates them.

items.title: Client applications
items.text: A client inside the network talking to a server elsewhere. They work today because NAT and firewall functions were designed for them.

items.title: Peer-to-peer applications
items.text: Hosts inside the network talking to hosts outside it. They often need a relay server, which turns the connection into two client/server connections.

items.title: Server applications
items.text: A server inside the network serving other people. They need port forwarding on the NAT, a global address and a stable DNS name.

cells: The hosts have to reach IPv6 on their own, mostly for peer-to-peer applications
All application types can be enabled; the gateway needs a prefix from the provider
The gateway tunnels IPv6 over IPv4, using 6to4 or configured tunnels
The provider must supply IPv4-over-IPv6 tunnels for the IPv4 hosts
